title: Pursuing a True Partnership
coreMove: A restaurant, or any organization, works best when the people making the product and the people delivering it share ownership of the guest's experience.

exampleSpecs.stakes: The traditional fine-dining structure puts the chef on top and treats service staff as subordinate, a hierarchy that quietly poisons both the kitchen and the dining room.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Accepting the general manager role at EMP in 2006 was conditional on a true partnership, not employment beneath a chef; refusing to merely work for someone was the entire point.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

exampleSpecs.stakes: The first move after taking the role was not issuing orders but aligning with the chef on running the place as equals before changing anything operationally.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

exampleSpecs.stakes: People in authority hold far more power over those beneath them than they realize, and a careless outburst that means nothing to the boss can stay with a young employee for years.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Decisions should be judged by what serves the whole restaurant, never by what wins for the kitchen or the floor as separate camps.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

exampleSpecs.stakes: The chef himself had asked for a fresh front-of-house leader and pointed to a specific candidate, so both sides wanted the same equal arrangement.
